title: Binary search
content:
Page 1
Binary Search
Source Material — Page 1
1. What is Binary Search?
Binary search is an efficient searching algorithm used to find a target value in a sorted collection. Instead of
checking every element one by one, it checks the middle element and eliminates half of the remaining search
range.
For n elements, linear search can require up to n checks. Binary search requires about logI(n) comparisons in
the worst case, making it useful for large sorted datasets.
2. Main Idea
At every step, compare the target with the middle element. If the middle value equals the target, the search
succeeds. If the middle value is smaller, search the right half. If it is larger, search the left half.
Example: In [3, 7, 12, 18, 25, 31, 42], to find 25, first inspect 18. Since 25 is greater than 18, ignore 18 and
everything before it, then search the right half.
3. Why Sorting is Necessary
The algorithm can discard a half only because the elements are ordered. In an unsorted array, comparing the
middle value does not tell us which half can safely be ignored.
4. Important Terms
low is the first index of the current search range. high is the last index. mid is the index of the element
currently being checked. The target is the value we are trying to find.

Page 2
Binary Search
Source Material — Page 2
5. Iterative Binary Search
The iterative version uses a loop. Initially, low = 0 and high = n − 1. While low is less than or equal to high,
calculate mid and compare A[mid] with the target.
Middle index: mid = low + (high − low) / 2. This form can avoid overflow that may occur with (low + high) / 2 in
fixed-size integer arithmetic.
Pseudocode
low = 0
high = n - 1
while low <= high:
    mid = low + (high - low) / 2
    if A[mid] == target: return mid
    else if A[mid] < target: low = mid + 1
    else: high = mid - 1
return -1
6. Step-by-Step Example
For A = [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56] and target = 23:
Step
low
high
mid
A[mid]
Action
1
0
7
3
12
Target is greater → right
2
4
7
5
23
Found

Page 3
Binary Search
Source Material — Page 3
7. Recursive Binary Search
Binary search can also be implemented recursively. The function receives the current low and high
boundaries. If low becomes greater than high, the range is empty and the target is absent.
Recursive pseudocode
binarySearch(A, low, high, target):
    if low > high: return -1
    mid = low + (high - low) / 2
    if A[mid] == target: return mid
    if A[mid] < target: search(mid + 1, high)
    else: search(low, mid - 1)
8. Missing Target
If the target is absent, the search range eventually becomes empty. In an iterative implementation this occurs
when low becomes greater than high. A program can return -1 to indicate that the target was not found.
Example: Search for 10 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16]. The middle value 8 is smaller, so move right. Then 12 is larger, so
move left. The range becomes empty, so 10 is absent.
9. Complexity
The best case is O(1), when the first middle element is the target. The average and worst-case time complexity
is O(log n). Iterative binary search uses O(1) extra space, while the usual recursive version uses O(log n)
call-stack space.
The logarithmic behavior comes from repeatedly halving the range: n → n/2 → n/4 → n/8 → …
10. Binary Search vs Linear Search
Linear search can work on unsorted data and has O(n) worst-case time. Binary search is faster for large sorted
arrays because it eliminates about half the candidates at each step, but it needs the ordering required to make
that elimination valid.

Page 4
Binary Search
Source Material — Page 4
11. Common Errors
Common mistakes include using binary search on unsorted data, choosing incorrect initial boundaries, using
the wrong loop condition, calculating mid incorrectly, and updating low or high incorrectly.
If A[mid] is smaller than the target, use low = mid + 1. If A[mid] is greater than the target, use high = mid − 1.
The middle index has already been checked, so it should not remain in the next range.
12. Duplicate Values
With duplicate values, ordinary binary search may return any index containing the target. Some problems
instead require the first or last occurrence.
To find the first occurrence, record a match and continue searching left. To find the last occurrence, record
a match and continue searching right.
13. Insertion Position
Binary search can find where a target should be inserted while keeping a sorted array ordered. This is often
called finding a lower bound or insertion position.
Example: In [2, 4, 7, 10], the insertion position for 6 is index 2, between 4 and 7.
14. When is Binary Search Useful?
Use it when the data is sorted or when the problem has a monotonic condition. It is common in sorted arrays,
ordered data, range problems, and optimization problems with a yes/no feasibility test.
15. Binary Search on an Answer
Sometimes the algorithm does not search for a value in an array. Instead, it searches a range of possible
answers. If all values below a boundary fail and all values at or above the boundary succeed, binary search
can locate that boundary.

Page 5
Binary Search
Source Material — Page 5
16. First Occurrence Example
For [1, 2, 2, 2, 5, 7] with target 2, ordinary binary search may stop at any 2. To find the first occurrence, store
the matching index and continue searching the left half using high = mid − 1. The smallest valid stored index is
the answer.
17. Last Occurrence Example
For the same array, to find the last occurrence, store the matching index and continue searching the right half
using low = mid + 1. The largest valid stored index is the answer.
18. Practical Checklist
Before applying binary search, ask: Is the data sorted or is the predicate monotonic? What are low and high?
What happens when A[mid] equals, is smaller than, or is greater than the target? What should be returned
when the target is absent? Do duplicates matter?
19. Key Takeaways
• Binary search repeatedly halves a valid search range.
• Basic array search normally requires sorted data.
• Worst-case time is O(log n).
• Iterative space is O(1).
• Boundary updates must exclude an already-checked middle element.
• Variants can find first/last occurrences, insertion positions, or an optimal boundary.
20. Final Worked Example
For A = [5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30] and target 20: start with low = 0 and high = 5. mid = 2 gives 15, so move right.
Now low = 3 and high = 5; mid = 4 gives 25, so move left. Finally mid = 3 gives 20, so the target is found at
index 3.

title: Biology
content: Biology is the scientific study of life and living organisms, exploring their structure, function, growth, origin, evolution, and distribution. It covers everything from the microscopic mechanics of cells and DNA to the complex interactions within massive ecosystems. At its core, biology is built on unifying principles like cell theory, which states that all living things are made of cells; genetics, the blueprint of heredity; and evolution, the process that drives the diversity of life on Earth. By studying biology, we gain a deeper understanding of the natural world and the vital processes that sustain human health, agriculture, and the global environment.

questions.question_text: What process drives the diversity of life on Earth?

title: History
content: History is the systematic study and documentation of past events, human experiences, and societal transformations over time. It relies on the rigorous analysis of diverse evidence, including written documents, oral traditions, artifacts, and archaeological discoveries, to reconstruct and interpret what happened in earlier eras. By exploring the complex political, economic, cultural, and social movements of the past, history helps us understand the roots of current global structures and human behavior. Ultimately, studying history allows us to identify repeating patterns and trace the long journey of human civilization, providing critical context for making informed decisions about the future.

questions.question_text: What does the study of history allow us to do that helps us make informed decisions about the future?
